supported_cases.query: What is a process address space?

claims.text: A process is a program in execution, and each process has its own address space. The operating system saves the process state in a process control block during a context switch.
Threads within the same process share code, data, and open files, providing concurrent execution within one address space.
Each thread has its own stack and registers, but all threads belonging to a single process operate within that process's shared address space.

Threads within the same process share code, data, and open files. This means all threads in a process operate within one common address space and can access the same program instructions, variables, and file descriptors.
Despite sharing those resources, each thread maintains its own stack and registers, so each thread has independent call state and CPU register values.
Threads provide concurrent execution within one address space, meaning multiple threads can make progress at the same time while reading and writing the same shared data.

Because threads share data, a race condition can occur when the result depends on the interleaving of concurrent accesses to that shared data. A mutex protects a critical section by allowing only one thread to enter at a time, preventing such races.
Deadlock occurs when a set of processes waits forever for resources held by another member of the set.
The four necessary deadlock conditions are: (1) mutual exclusion, (2) hold and wait, (3) no preemption, and (4) circular wait. All four must hold simultaneously for a deadlock to occur.
In round robin scheduling, each ready process is given a fixed time quantum — a predetermined amount of CPU time during which it may execute.
When a process's time quantum expires, that running process is moved to the back of the ready queue, allowing the next process in line to receive its own quantum.

supported_cases.query: How does a mutex protect a critical section?

claims.text: A race condition occurs when the result depends on the interleaving of concurrent accesses to shared data. In other words, if two threads read or write the same data at the same time, the final outcome can change depending on which thread's operations happen first.

A mutex protects a critical section by allowing only one thread to enter at a time. This means that while one thread is inside the critical section, any other thread that tries to enter must wait until the first thread exits, preventing the interleaving that causes race conditions.
